title: Passover
summary: Exodus 12 presents the first Passover on the night Israel is about to leave Egypt. Each household shares a meal, marks its doorway with blood, and eats ready to travel; the narrative links this sign with the death of Egypt's firstborn and Israel's protection. Unleavened bread and the memory of the night become part of an annual practice for telling the next generation how the people were freed. Passover is therefore both a story of escape and a ritual that teaches Israel who it is.
historical_context: The Exodus account locates Passover within the final confrontation with Pharaoh and the departure from Egypt. Its instructions describe a household meal, unleavened bread, marked doorways, and readiness to leave. The text later connects the observance with Israel's life in the land and with teaching children about the rescue. These are the biblical narrative's own details; the sources listed here do not independently establish a date for the exodus or the ritual's development.
literary_context: Exodus 12 interweaves instructions for the meal with the story of the final plague and departure, so the ritual is explained through the event it remembers. Exodus 13 then makes remembrance a practice for future generations, including a parent's explanation to a child. Deuteronomy 16 retells the observance for Israel's life in the land, linking the festival to its central worship setting. The texts preserve both the rescue story and later instructions for keeping its memory.
covenantal_significance: Passover marks Israel's rescue and gives households a recurring way to remember it. In Exodus, the meal is tied to the people's protection and departure; later instructions make remembrance and teaching part of communal identity. New Testament writers reuse Passover language in distinct ways: Luke places the meal in Jesus' final night, Paul calls Christ “our Passover,” and John situates Jesus' death within Passover time. These later readings are Christian interpretations of the tradition and do not replace the festival's meaning in Israel's story.
canonical_role: Passover becomes a central memory of Israel's deliverance, repeated in Deuteronomy and observed in later biblical stories. The New Testament returns to it when narrating Jesus' final meal and death, with Paul explicitly applying the image to Christ. Reading these passages together reveals a developing tradition: the Exodus rescue remains the starting point, while later Christian texts interpret it in relation to Jesus.

related_objects.notes: Places Passover within the exodus-to-Sinai timeline anchor.

interpretive_notes.note: Passover is not only about escape; it also forms identity, memory, and worship.
The New Testament does not erase Passover; it rereads it through the crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus.
